Half of that is good advice. EF Core's performance guide tells you to always prefer asynchronous APIs, because synchronous ones block a thread for the whole database round trip.

Async is about the thread, not the rows
EF Core's async docs say async operations avoid blocking a thread while the query runs, and have the same effects as their sync counterparts.

, which can only complete once the last row is in the list. That's what EF's guide calls buffering: all results loaded into memory, so memory grows with the row count. In a test with EF Core 10 on SQL Server LocalDB, 200,000 orders with a 100-character note each kept about 115 MB on the managed heap, and the first row was available only after about 1.4 seconds, when the whole result had arrived.
Streaming hands you one row at a time
means EF gives you one result at a time and never holds the whole set. The guide puts it this way: in principle, a streaming query needs the same memory for one row or a thousand.
streams. In the same test, a no-tracking stream grew the heap by less than 1 MB, and the first row arrived after about 0.1 seconds.
The change tracker is a second buffer
